capstone: Capstone: multi-file text-processing utility in C11. Build 'wfreq', a word-frequency counter that streams arbitrarily large text files in constant memory, stores results in a dynamically grown hash table of heap-allocated strings, and writes a sorted report to an output file. Requirements: at least four translation units (main, table, io, util) plus headers, built by a Makefile you write with debug and release targets; clean under gcc -Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c11 -pedantic; zero reports from AddressSanitizer and UBSan on a 1 GB input and on malformed inputs (empty file, no trailing newline, 10 MB single line, binary bytes); every allocation and I/O call checked; a README explaining your ownership conventions and how you debugged at least one real bug with gdb.
disclaimer: Original study guide keyed to public curriculum; course content itself lives at the source.

checkpoints: Without compiling: two files, a.c and b.c, each contain 'int counter = 0;' at file scope and both are linked into one program. State what the linker will do and why, then build it to verify your prediction.

Explain in your own words why a declaration may appear in many translation units while a definition must appear in exactly one, and name one example of each from the C standard library (for instance, the printf declaration in <stdio.h> versus its definition inside libc).
keyConcepts: Translation phases: preprocessing, compilation, assembly, linking
Preprocessor as textual expansion: #include, #define, #ifdef/#ifndef, #error
Include guards and #pragma once idiom
Declarations versus definitions
External vs internal linkage (extern, static)
One definition per program expectation for external symbols
Object files, symbol tables, and the linker's job
Static libraries and link order basics
labs: Write a two-file program (main.c calling add() declared in calc.h and defined in calc.c). Compile each file with 'gcc -c', then link the .o files manually. Run 'nm' on each object file and identify which symbols are defined (T/D) versus undefined (U).

Run 'gcc -E' on a file that includes <stdio.h> and pipe the output to 'wc -l' to see how much text one include pulls in. Then write a small header with and without an include guard, include it twice from one .c file, and observe the compile error the unguarded version produces.

Deliberately place a non-static function definition in a header included by two .c files, link them, and record the linker's 'multiple definition' error. Fix it by moving the definition into exactly one .c file and leaving only the declaration in the header.
Compile a simple program with 'gcc -S -O0' and read the generated .s file: find the function label, the prologue, a call instruction to a library function, and the return sequence.
objectives: Describe the four logical translation phases: preprocessing, compilation to assembly, assembly to object code, and linking.
Use preprocessor directives (#include, #define, #ifdef, include guards) correctly and explain that inclusion is textual expansion.
Separate declarations from definitions across headers and source files to avoid multiple-definition linker errors.
Produce and inspect intermediate artifacts: preprocessed output (-E), assembly (-S), and object-file symbol tables (nm).
modules.title: Module 1: The Translation Pipeline — From Source to Executable

checkpoints: Given 'int *p = malloc(4 * sizeof *p);' explain in writing why 'sizeof *p' is more maintainable than 'sizeof(int)', then change the allocation to zero-initialized memory with calloc and justify when zero-initialization matters.

Run your Lab 2 vector under AddressSanitizer with a driver that pushes 10,000 elements and pops them all: it must report zero errors, and you must be able to point at the exact line where each allocation is released.
keyConcepts: Pointers as typed addresses: address-of (&) and dereference (*)
Pointer arithmetic scales by sizeof the pointed-to type
void* as a generic address carrier; NULL and null-pointer constants
Automatic, static, and allocated storage durations and object lifetimes
malloc / calloc / realloc / free semantics and failure handling
The safe realloc idiom: assign to a temporary, check for NULL first
Dangling pointers, double free, use-after-free
Ownership conventions: who allocates, who frees, const-qualified pointers
labs: Write a program that reads a size from stdin, validates it, allocates an int array with malloc, fills and prints it, then frees it. Compile with -Wall -Wextra and fix every warning before running.

Implement a growable vector of double using realloc with doubling growth. Use the safe pattern: 'double *tmp = realloc(v, newsize); if (!tmp) { handle; } v = tmp;'. Write a test driver that pushes 1,000 values.

Write two small buggy programs: one that leaks memory in a loop and one that calls free twice on the same pointer. Build both with -fsanitize=address and record the exact diagnostic each sanitizer report gives you.
Write a function that returns a pointer to a local variable. Compile without -w, read the -Wreturn-local-addr warning, then fix the design by switching to caller-provided storage.
objectives: Explain what a pointer value is (an address plus a type) and how pointer arithmetic scales by the size of the pointed-to type.
Allocate, reallocate, and free heap memory with malloc/calloc/realloc/free, checking every allocation for failure.
Distinguish automatic, static, and allocated storage durations and predict how long each object lives.
Implement ownership conventions (who allocates, who frees) that prevent leaks, double frees, and use-after-free.
modules.title: Module 2: Pointers and Dynamic Memory

checkpoints: Hand-trace this: 'char a[10]; char *p = a;'. List which of sizeof(a), sizeof(p), &a, a+1, and &a+1 differ from each other and why. Verify with a small printing program.
Write a function 'void reverse(char *s)' that reverses a string in place using no <string.h> calls except strlen, then prove it handles the empty string and a single-character string correctly.
keyConcepts: Array-to-pointer decay and its three exceptions (sizeof, &, string-literal initialization)
sizeof on arrays versus on pointers
String literals live in read-only storage; char arrays are writable copies
NUL terminator discipline and off-by-one sizing (strlen + 1)
Bounded string functions and their pitfalls (strncpy may not terminate)
snprintf as the safe formatting workhorse
Multidimensional arrays are row-major contiguous blocks
Variable-length arrays: convenience versus stack-overflow risk
labs: Write a program that prints sizeof for 'char buf[64];' and for a 'char *p' pointing at it. Explain the different results in a code comment stating the decay rule.
Implement a safe line reader: fgets into a fixed buffer, detect a missing newline to grow the buffer dynamically, and handle EOF. Test it on a 10 KB single-line input and on an empty file.

Take a program that uses strcpy/strcat and rewrite it with snprintf/strncat using explicit size math. Construct a test input where the unbounded version overflows and show the bounded version truncating safely instead.
Write 'char *s = "literal"; s[0] = 'x';', build and run it, observe the crash, then fix it by declaring a writable char array instead.
objectives: Explain when an array decays to a pointer and when it does not (sizeof, unary &, string-literal initialization).
Manipulate C strings as NUL-terminated char arrays using <string.h> safely, with bounded operations and explicit length checks.
Compare stack arrays, variable-length arrays, and heap arrays, and choose correctly for a given size and lifetime.
Write functions that take array parameters together with explicit size arguments instead of trusting a bare pointer.
modules.title: Module 3: Arrays and Strings

checkpoints: On a typical 64-bit ABI, compute by hand the sizeof and each member offsetof for 'struct { char a; int b; char c; }', then verify with a program that prints offsetof for all three members.

Explain in writing why reading a union member other than the one most recently stored is fragile, and describe the tagged-union discipline (a kind field checked before every access) that makes unions safe.
keyConcepts: struct layout: member order, alignment, and padding
offsetof and reasoning about member addresses
Designated initializers and compound literals
Anonymous structs and unions (C11)
Unions as space-efficient variant storage; tagged (discriminated) unions
Enums: named integer constants, promotion rules, state machines
Bit-fields: what they guarantee and why they are non-portable
Flexible array members for variable-length trailing data
labs: Define 'struct { char a; double b; char c; int d; }', print sizeof and offsetof of each member, then reorder members to 'char, char, int, double' and compare: compute the bytes saved and explain where the padding went.

Implement a tagged union 'Value' with an int kind field and a union of { long i; double d; char *s; }. Write make/print/free functions that switch on kind, freeing the string member only when kind says it is a string.
Build an enum-driven state machine for a word counter with states START, IN_WORD, IN_SPACE, fed character by character through a transition function.
Use a flexible array member struct to model a variable-length packet: allocate it with a single malloc of sizeof(struct) + payload bytes and demonstrate writing and reading the payload.
objectives: Define structs, use the . and -> operators, and initialize with designated initializers and compound literals.
Predict struct size and member offsets from alignment rules, and reorder members to minimize padding.
Use unions for space-efficient variant storage and apply the tagged-union discipline to access them safely.
Model state machines and option sets with enums and apply integer-promotion rules correctly.
modules.title: Module 4: Structs, Unions, and Enums

checkpoints: Explain the bug in 'while (!feof(f)) { fgets(buf, sizeof buf, f); process(buf); }', rewrite the loop so the read itself controls iteration, and test both versions on a file whose last line has no trailing newline.
Write a function that safely replaces a file's contents: write to a temporary file, fflush, then rename it over the original. Explain in writing why each step matters for crash safety.
keyConcepts: FILE* streams: fopen modes (r/w/a, + for update, b for binary)
Buffering: fully buffered, line buffered, unbuffered; setvbuf and fflush
Line-oriented input with fgets versus block I/O with fread/fwrite
The feof/ferror discipline: the read call, not feof, controls the loop
errno, perror, and strerror for diagnosing failures
Format-string safety: never pass untrusted data as the format argument
File positioning: fseek, ftell, rewind, fgetpos/fsetpos
Streaming design: processing files larger than RAM in constant memory
labs: Write a wc-like tool counting bytes, words, and lines from stdin or a named file. Test on: an empty file, a file with no trailing newline, and a 1 GB generated file, confirming constant memory use.
Write 1,000 fixed-layout records to a binary file with fwrite, then read back record #500 by seeking to offset 500 * sizeof(record) with fseek. Verify the contents match what you wrote.
Write a file-copy program using fread/fwrite with a 64 KB buffer. Compare sha256sum of source and copy, then extend the program to correctly handle a short write from fwrite.
Write a program that passes a user-supplied string as the printf format argument, observe the -Wformat-security warning, then fix it by using '%s' with the string as an argument.
objectives: Open, read, write, and close files with the <stdio.h> stream API, checking every call for failure.
Distinguish text versus binary mode, buffered versus unbuffered I/O, and line-oriented versus block-oriented reads.
Handle I/O errors robustly: check ferror/feof, report with perror/strerror, and never treat a short read as EOF.
Use file positioning (fseek/ftell/rewind) and write streaming programs that handle files larger than RAM.
modules.title: Module 5: File I/O

checkpoints: Given the link error 'undefined reference to sqrt', state the exact fix and explain why '-lm' must appear after the object files on the gcc command line.
From memory, write a minimal correct Makefile for main.c + util.c + util.h with separate debug (CFLAGS_DEBUG) and release (CFLAGS_RELEASE) flag sets, then verify it builds both.
keyConcepts: Separate compilation: -c to object files, then an explicit link step
Include paths (-I) and library paths (-L); link order ('-l' after the objects that need it)
Warning flags: -Wall -Wextra -Werror; standards: -std=c11 -pedantic
Debug info (-g) versus optimization levels (-O0 through -O3, -Os)
Sanitizers as standard workflow: -fsanitize=address,undefined
Make: targets, prerequisites, recipes; automatic variables $@ $< $^
Pattern rules (%.o: %.c), variables (CC, CFLAGS), .PHONY targets
Incremental rebuilds: why make rebuilds only what changed
labs: Take a three-file project and build it three ways: a single gcc invocation, manual 'gcc -c' steps plus an explicit link, and a Makefile you write. Confirm all three produce the same program behavior.
Write a Makefile with a pattern rule '%.o: %.c', CC/CFLAGS variables, and a .PHONY clean target. Demonstrate that touching one .c file rebuilds only its .o and then relinks.
Take a warning-laden program and iterate with '-Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c11 -pedantic' until it builds clean. Keep a log of each warning fixed and what it was telling you.
Build your Module 2 vector program with '-fsanitize=address,undefined -g', run your test driver, fix every report, then rebuild with '-O2 -DNDEBUG' and compare runtime on a large input.
objectives: Compile and link multi-file projects from the command line with explicit -c, -o, -I, -L, and -l steps in the correct order.
Use warning and language-standard flags (-Wall -Wextra -Werror -std=c11 -pedantic) and explain what each major class catches.
Write a Makefile with targets, prerequisites, recipes, variables, and pattern rules, and explain the TAB-before-recipe rule.
Apply -g, optimization levels, and sanitizers (-fsanitize=address,undefined) as a standard debug and hardening workflow.
modules.title: Module 6: Build Tooling — gcc Flags and make

checkpoints: From a gdb backtrace of a three-deep call stack, use 'frame N' and 'info locals' to identify which frame holds the buggy variable and display its value. Do this on your Lab 1 crashing program.
Explain in writing why debugging at -O2 shows 'optimized out' variables and jumping line numbers, and state the standard practice: debug at -O0, ship at -O2.
keyConcepts: Debug info with -g; why -O0 is the debugging optimization level
Core workflow: break, run, next, step, finish, continue
Inspecting state: print, x (examine memory), info locals, info args
Backtraces and frames: bt, frame N, up/down
Watchpoints: stopping when a variable changes
Conditional breakpoints for bugs that appear on iteration 999 of 1000
Core dumps: ulimit -c, loading a core without re-running
Sanitizer output plus gdb: two tools, one bug-localization workflow
labs: Write a program with an off-by-one write past a stack array that segfaults. Run it under gdb, capture the backtrace, identify the faulting line and variable values, then fix the bug.

Debug a use-after-free: set a breakpoint after free(), place a watchpoint on the pointer variable, and step through to observe the stale access. Fix it with the set-pointer-to-NULL-after-free discipline.
Enable core dumps ('ulimit -c unlimited'), crash a program, then load the core file in gdb and produce the backtrace without re-running the program.
Debug a silent logic bug (wrong output, no crash): use a conditional breakpoint to stop only on the failing iteration of a loop that processes 1,000 records.
objectives: Build with -g and drive gdb through its core workflow: run, break, next/step/finish, continue, print, backtrace.
Inspect memory directly with the x command, watch variables with watchpoints, and examine frames and locals.
Debug crashes: obtain a backtrace from a segfault, identify the faulting line, and distinguish null dereference from heap corruption.
Combine gdb with core dumps and sanitizer output to localize bugs faster.
modules.title: Module 7: Debugging with gdb

checkpoints: Classify each as undefined, unspecified, or implementation-defined behavior, with a one-sentence justification: (a) x = x++ (b) the order in which function arguments are evaluated (c) sizeof(int) (d) dereferencing a null pointer (e) shifting a 32-bit int left by 32.
Explain in writing why 'it works on my machine' is not evidence of correctness for a program containing undefined behavior, citing one optimizer behavior you personally observed in these labs.
keyConcepts: The three behavior classes: undefined vs unspecified vs implementation-defined
Why the compiler may assume UB never happens — and optimizes on that assumption
Major UB classes: bad dereference, out-of-bounds, lifetime errors, signed overflow
Uninitialized reads, data races, and modifying a variable twice between sequence points
Strict aliasing and effective type
Detection tooling: UBSan, ASan, -Wall -Wextra, -fanalyzer where available
Checked arithmetic and explicit bounds as defensive patterns
Safe-coding discipline: initialize at declaration, validate inputs, check every fallible call
labs: Write a program that adds two ints read from stdin. Trigger signed overflow, capture the UBSan report with -fsanitize=undefined, then rewrite with a checked-add that detects overflow before it can happen.
Write snippets like 'i = i++ + ++i;' and 'a[i] = i++;', compile with -Wall -Wsequence-point, read the warnings, then rewrite each using explicit temporaries with well-defined evaluation order.
Write a strict-aliasing violation (store through an int*, read the same storage through a float*), compare behavior at -O0 versus -O2, then fix it with memcpy or a union and confirm the fix at -O2.
Run a full hardening pass on your Module 5 file tool: -Wall -Wextra -Werror, ASan+UBSan clean on hostile inputs, every allocation and I/O call checked, all inputs validated.
objectives: Define undefined behavior and explain why the compiler is permitted to assume it never happens, with optimization consequences.

Recognize the major UB classes: invalid dereference, out-of-bounds access, use-after-free/double-free, signed integer overflow, uninitialized reads, data races, strict-aliasing violations, and unsequenced modifications.
Use UBSan, ASan, compiler warnings, and static analysis to detect UB during development instead of in production.
Apply safe-coding discipline: initialize at declaration, validate all inputs, bound every loop and copy, check every fallible call, prefer size-aware APIs.
modules.title: Module 8: Undefined Behavior and Safe-Coding Discipline

objectives: Explain the four stages of C translation and how the preprocessor, compiler, and linker cooperate to produce an executable.
Manage dynamic memory safely with malloc/calloc/realloc/free, and diagnose the classic lifetime bugs: leaks, double free, and use-after-free.
Use pointers, arrays, strings, structs, unions, and enums fluently while reasoning about object representation, alignment, and padding.
Build, debug, and harden small C programs with gcc flags, Makefiles, gdb, sanitizers, and a working knowledge of undefined behavior classes.
